title: Mahmud of Ghazni raids India
summary: Mahmud, the Turkic ruler of the Ghaznavid state based at Ghazni in today's Afghanistan, leads a long series of raids into northern India, traditionally counted as seventeen. He defeats the Hindu Shahi and other Indian kings and plunders wealthy cities and temples, including Mathura, Kannauj and, in 1025, the temple of Somnath in Gujarat, carrying the treasure back to Ghazni.
significance: The raids made the Punjab part of the Ghaznavid realm and opened the way for later Muslim rulers in northern India, while the sack of Somnath remains a much-remembered and contested episode in Indian memory.

title: The Tale of Genji
summary: Murasaki Shikibu, a lady-in-waiting at the Japanese imperial court, writes a long prose narrative about the loves and losses of a prince, Genji, and his descendants. Written in Japanese in the phonetic kana script used by court women, it runs to 54 chapters and was already being read at court by 1008.
significance: Often called the world's first novel, it is the central classic of Japanese literature and a detailed picture of Heian court life.

title: First government paper money
summary: In Sichuan, where heavy iron coins are used, merchants in Chengdu have begun issuing paper notes that can be exchanged for coin. In 1024 the Song government takes over the business and issues the notes, called jiaozi, itself.
significance: It was the first paper currency issued by a state anywhere; paper money spread through China and astonished later visitors such as Marco Polo.

title: Avicenna's Canon of Medicine

location.name: Hamadan (approximate; Avicenna wrote it over many years in several Persian cities)

summary: Ibn Sina, known in Europe as Avicenna, a Persian physician and philosopher, completes his Canon of Medicine, a five-volume medical encyclopedia written in Arabic. It brings together Greek medicine from Hippocrates and Galen, the work of physicians of the Islamic world and his own observations, covering anatomy, diseases, drugs and how to test medicines.
significance: Translated into Latin in the 12th century, the Canon became a standard medical textbook in the Islamic world and in European universities, still used in some places in the 1600s.

title: Seljuk Empire
summary: The Seljuks, Turkic nomads who had converted to Sunni Islam, conquered Iran and Iraq and took Baghdad in 1055, ruling as sultans in the caliph's name. Their victory over Byzantium at Manzikert opened Anatolia to Turkish settlement.
significance: They began the long era of Turkic rule in the Middle East, revived Sunni institutions, and their advance into Anatolia prompted the First Crusade.

title: Western Xia
summary: The Tanguts, a people related to the Tibetans, founded an empire in what is now Ningxia and Gansu, controlling the corridor that linked China to Central Asia. Their rulers devised a script of their own, patronized Buddhism and fought the Song to a standstill, until the Mongols destroyed the state in the campaign during which Genghis Khan died.
significance: For two centuries Western Xia was the third power of China alongside the Song and the Liao or Jin, and thousands of texts in its script survive.

title: Bi Sheng invents movable type
summary: Bi Sheng, a commoner of the Song dynasty, makes individual characters out of baked clay, sets them in a frame with wax and resin to print a page, and reuses them afterward. The only account is by the scholar Shen Kuo, written some decades later; with thousands of characters to handle, woodblock printing stayed more common in China.
significance: It is the first known printing with movable type, four centuries before Gutenberg; the idea was developed further in Korea with metal type.

title: Great Schism between East and West
summary: Envoys from Rome lay a papal bull excommunicating Michael Cerularius, patriarch of Constantinople, on the altar of Hagia Sophia, and the patriarch excommunicates them in return. The quarrel is over the pope's claim to authority over the whole Church and over differences in creed and practice. Historians see the split as a gradual process rather than a single event, and it hardens over the following centuries, especially after crusaders sack Constantinople in 1204.
significance: Christianity divided into the Roman Catholic Church in the West and the Eastern Orthodox churches, a division that still exists, although the mutual excommunications of 1054 were lifted in 1965.

title: Norman conquest of England

location.name: Battle, East Sussex (site of the Battle of Hastings)

summary: William, Duke of Normandy, claims the English throne, lands an army in Sussex and defeats and kills King Harold II at the Battle of Hastings in October 1066. He is crowned in Westminster Abbey on Christmas Day and spends the next years crushing rebellions and replacing the English nobility with Norman and French lords.
significance: The conquest tied England closely to France and continental Europe, brought a French-speaking ruling class and a wave of castle building, and added thousands of French words to the English language.

title: Battle of Manzikert
summary: A Seljuk Turkish army under Sultan Alp Arslan defeats the Byzantine army of Emperor Romanos IV Diogenes near Manzikert, in eastern Anatolia, and captures the emperor. Byzantine losses in the battle itself are probably modest, but civil war follows in the empire, and Turkish groups move into Anatolia largely unopposed.
significance: Within a decade much of Anatolia was under Turkish rule, beginning its long transformation into a Turkish land, and Byzantine appeals for help contributed to the First Crusade.

title: Shen Kuo describes the magnetic compass
summary: In retirement, the Song official and polymath Shen Kuo writes the Dream Pool Essays, notes on everything from astronomy and fossils to printing. In it he describes a magnetized needle that points south, and notes that it points slightly away from true south.
significance: It is the first clear description of a magnetic compass and of magnetic declination; within decades Chinese sailors were steering by the needle.

title: University of Bologna founded
summary: Students in Bologna, in northern Italy, gather around teachers of Roman law and form associations to hire their masters and protect their own rights. The year 1088 was chosen in the 1880s as a symbolic founding date; the university grew gradually and has no single founding act.
significance: Bologna is often called the oldest university in continuous operation, and its model of a self-governing community of scholars helped shape the universities that spread across Europe and later the world.

title: Crusades in the Holy Land
summary: Successive Latin Christian expeditions fought for control of places in the eastern Mediterranean, establishing crusader states and confronting Muslim powers. The band runs from the First Crusade to the fall of Acre; crusading elsewhere continued beyond this interval.
significance: The crusades deepened the divide between Latin Christians, Eastern Christians and Muslims, while the contact they brought increased Mediterranean trade and the flow of learning into Europe.

title: First Crusade
summary: Answering Pope Urban II's call in 1095 to help the Byzantine Empire against the Seljuk Turks and to win back Jerusalem, armies of knights and commoners from western Europe march east. After capturing Nicaea and Antioch, they take Jerusalem in July 1099 and massacre many of its Muslim and Jewish inhabitants.
significance: The crusaders founded states in the Levant that lasted nearly two centuries, and the crusades left a lasting legacy of hostility and mistrust between Western Christians, Muslims and Eastern Christians.

title: Kingdom of Zimbabwe
summary: Great Zimbabwe was the capital of a Shona kingdom on the plateau between the Zambezi and Limpopo rivers. Its rulers lived within massive dry-stone walls and grew rich on cattle and on gold and ivory traded to the Swahili coast.
significance: Its stone ruins are the largest ancient structures in Africa south of the Sahara, and the modern country of Zimbabwe is named after them.

title: Angkor Wat built
summary: King Suryavarman II of the Khmer Empire begins building Angkor Wat at his capital, Angkor, in today's Cambodia, as a vast temple to the Hindu god Vishnu, probably also meant as his own funerary temple. Its towers represent Mount Meru, home of the gods, and its walls are carved with scenes from Hindu epics. Work seems to stop around the time of the king's death, with some carvings left unfinished.
significance: Later turned into a Buddhist temple, Angkor Wat is one of the largest religious monuments in the world and appears on Cambodia's national flag.

title: Jin dynasty (Jurchen)
summary: The Jurchen, a people of Manchuria, rose against their Khitan overlords under Aguda, destroyed the Liao and in 1127 took northern China from the Song. They ruled it from what is now Beijing and later from Kaifeng, until the Mongols, allied with the Southern Song, wiped the dynasty out.
significance: The Jin confined the Song to southern China for a century; the Manchus who founded the Qing dynasty were descendants of the Jurchen.

title: Jurchens capture the Song capital
summary: Armies of the Jurchen Jin dynasty take Kaifeng, the Song capital, and carry off Emperor Qinzong, his father the retired emperor Huizong and thousands of members of the court. A prince who escapes re-establishes the dynasty in the south, with its capital at Hangzhou.
significance: The Song lost northern China for good, and the wealth and population of China shifted decisively to the south.

title: Genpei War
summary: The Minamoto and Taira clans fought for power in Japan. Minamoto victory at Dan-no-ura helped establish warrior government and laid the groundwork for the Kamakura shogunate.
significance: It ended the dominance of the imperial court and began the rule of the samurai, and its battles became the subject of The Tale of the Heike.

title: Zhu Xi's Neo-Confucianism

location.name: Wuyi Mountains, Fujian (where Zhu Xi taught)

summary: The Song scholar Zhu Xi publishes his commentaries on four Confucian texts, the Analects, the Mencius, the Great Learning and the Doctrine of the Mean, which he groups as the Four Books. His teaching joins Confucian ethics to an account of the universe that answers Buddhist and Taoist ideas.
significance: From 1313 his commentaries were the required basis of China's civil service examinations, and his school became the orthodoxy of Korea and Tokugawa Japan as well.

title: Kamakura shogunate
summary: A military government centered at Kamakura governed Japan alongside the imperial court. This band begins with Yoritomo's appointment as shogun in 1192; historians also date the regime's emergence to 1185.
significance: It was Japan's first government of warriors, beginning nearly seven centuries in which shoguns, not emperors, held real power.

title: Rapa Nui and the moai
summary: Polynesian voyagers settle Rapa Nui (Easter Island), one of the most remote inhabited islands on Earth, probably around 1200, though estimates vary. Over the next few centuries they carve nearly a thousand giant stone statues, the moai, mostly from the volcanic rock of the Rano Raraku quarry, and set many of them on stone platforms, probably to honor ancestors.
significance: The moai are among the best-known monuments of the Pacific, and how the islanders moved them and what happened to their society afterward are still debated by archaeologists.

title: Delhi Sultanate
summary: A succession of five Turkic and Afghan dynasties ruled much of northern India from Delhi. The sultans held off the Mongols, at times extended their rule deep into the south, and were finally overthrown by Babur in 1526.
significance: The sultanate established lasting Muslim rule in India and fostered an Indo-Islamic culture in architecture, language and music.

title: Genghis Khan unites the Mongols

location.name: Onon River headwaters (approximate site of the assembly)

summary: Temujin, a Mongol chief who has spent years defeating and absorbing rival tribes, is proclaimed Genghis Khan at a great assembly, a kurultai, near the Onon River. He reorganizes the steppe peoples into an army divided into units of ten, a hundred and a thousand, loyal to him rather than to their clans.
significance: Genghis Khan and his successors built the Mongol Empire, the largest contiguous land empire in history, which at its height stretched from Korea to eastern Europe and linked East and West through conquest and trade.

title: Mongol Empire
summary: Genghis Khan united the Mongol tribes in 1206, and he and his successors conquered lands from Korea to Hungary, including China, Central Asia, Iran and Russia. After 1260 the empire divided into four khanates that still recognized a common heritage.
significance: It was the largest contiguous land empire in history; its conquests killed millions but also linked East and West through trade, travel and the exchange of ideas.

title: Magna Carta
summary: At Runnymede, by the River Thames, rebel barons force King John of England to agree to a charter limiting royal power, including the promise that no free man will be imprisoned or punished except by the lawful judgment of his peers or the law of the land. The pope annuls it within months and civil war follows, but revised versions are reissued in 1216, 1217 and 1225.
significance: Magna Carta became a lasting symbol of the idea that rulers are subject to the law, inspiring later English, American and international ideas of rights and constitutional government.

title: Mali Empire
summary: Founded by Sundiata Keita, the Mali Empire controlled the gold fields and trade routes of the upper Niger. Under Mansa Musa in the 14th century it was famous across the Islamic world for its wealth, and Timbuktu became a center of trade and scholarship.
significance: Mali was the largest and richest state of medieval West Africa and a main source of the gold that reached the Mediterranean world.

title: Golden Horde
summary: The Golden Horde was the western khanate of the Mongol Empire, founded by Batu, a grandson of Genghis Khan. From the lower Volga it ruled the steppe and took tribute from the Russian principalities, and its khans adopted Islam in the 14th century.
significance: Its two centuries of dominance shaped the rise of Moscow, which grew powerful as its tax collector and then replaced it.

title: Mamluk Sultanate
summary: The Mamluks were soldiers of slave origin, mostly Turkic and Circassian, who seized power in Egypt and ruled it and Syria from Cairo. They defeated the Mongols at Ain Jalut and expelled the last crusaders from the Levant.
significance: For more than 250 years they made Cairo the political and cultural capital of the Arab world, until the Ottomans conquered them in 1517.

title: Tripitaka Koreana completed

location.name: Haeinsa temple (where the blocks are kept)

summary: With the Mongols invading and the court of Goryeo sheltering on Ganghwa Island, Korean monks finish carving the whole Buddhist canon onto more than 80,000 wooden printing blocks, a task of sixteen years undertaken as a plea for divine protection. The blocks have been stored at the temple of Haeinsa since 1398.
significance: It is the most complete and accurate surviving edition of the Buddhist scriptures in Chinese characters, and the blocks can still be printed from.

title: Mongols sack Baghdad
summary: A Mongol army led by Hulagu, a grandson of Genghis Khan, besieges Baghdad and takes it after the caliph surrenders. The city is sacked, the last Abbasid caliph of Baghdad, al-Mustasim, is executed, and very many inhabitants are killed; estimates range from tens of thousands to the far higher figures given by medieval chroniclers.
significance: The sack ended the Abbasid Caliphate in Baghdad and the city's role as the political center of the Islamic world, although a line of Abbasid caliphs survived as figureheads under the Mamluks in Cairo.

title: Battle of Ain Jalut
summary: The Mamluk army of Egypt, under Sultan Qutuz and his commander Baybars, defeats a Mongol force in the Jezreel Valley, in today's northern Israel. Most of the Mongol army has withdrawn after the death of the Great Khan Mongke, leaving a smaller force under the general Kitbuqa, who is killed.
significance: The victory stopped the Mongol advance toward Egypt, secured the Mamluk Sultanate in Egypt and Syria for over 250 years, and showed that the Mongols could be beaten in open battle.

title: Yuan dynasty
summary: Kublai Khan, grandson of Genghis Khan, proclaimed the Yuan dynasty and completed the Mongol conquest of China in 1279, ruling from Dadu, now Beijing. The Mongols kept themselves apart from their Chinese subjects, and rebellions drove them back to the steppe in 1368.
significance: It was the first time all of China was ruled by a foreign people, and under it travel between China and Europe became possible, as in the journeys of Marco Polo.

title: Mongol invasions of Japan
summary: Kublai Khan twice sends fleets carrying Mongol, Chinese and Korean troops against Japan after it refuses to submit. Both land at Hakata Bay on Kyushu, where samurai resist them, and both are wrecked by storms; the second, in 1281, is one of the largest seaborne invasions before modern times.
significance: Japan stayed outside the Mongol Empire, and the storms were remembered as kamikaze, divine winds, protecting the country; the cost of defense weakened the Kamakura shogunate.

title: Marco Polo in China
summary: The Venetian merchant Marco Polo reaches the court of Kublai Khan with his father and uncle and, by his own account, spends seventeen years in the khan's service, travelling widely in China. Back in Italy, he dictates his story to a fellow prisoner of war around 1298. Some historians have doubted parts of it, but most accept that he made the journey.
significance: His book gave Europeans their first detailed picture of China and the East, and it was read closely by later explorers, including Columbus.

title: Yuan dynasty conquers the Song

location.name: Yamen, Guangdong (site of the last Song battle; approximate)

summary: Kublai Khan, a grandson of Genghis Khan who has proclaimed the Yuan dynasty in 1271, completes the decades-long Mongol conquest of the Southern Song. At the naval Battle of Yamen, off China's southern coast, the last Song forces are destroyed, and an official carrying the child emperor jumps into the sea with him.
significance: All of China was now ruled by Mongol conquerors, and under the Yuan it became part of a wider Mongol world that eased travel between China and the West, as in the journeys described by Marco Polo.

title: Majapahit
summary: Majapahit was a Hindu-Buddhist kingdom of eastern Java that, under King Hayam Wuruk and his minister Gajah Mada in the 14th century, claimed authority over much of the Indonesian archipelago and the Malay Peninsula.
significance: It was the largest of the pre-Islamic states of island Southeast Asia, and modern Indonesia looks back to it as a forerunner of national unity.

title: Ottoman Empire
summary: From a small principality in northwestern Anatolia, the Ottomans conquered the Balkans, took Constantinople in 1453 and went on to rule the Middle East, North Africa and southeastern Europe. The empire declined in the 19th century and was dissolved after its defeat in World War I.
significance: For six centuries it was one of the world's great powers and the leading state of the Islamic world, and its breakup produced the modern map of the Middle East and the Balkans.

title: Renaissance (approx.)
summary: A revival of classical learning and new approaches to art, scholarship, and humanism spread from Italian cities across Europe. Its timing varied by region, so the band represents a broad convention rather than fixed boundaries.
significance: It changed how Europeans thought about art, learning and human ability, and prepared the way for the Scientific Revolution and the modern world.

title: Mansa Musa's pilgrimage to Mecca

location.name: Timbuktu (representative; the pilgrimage went via Cairo to Mecca)

summary: Mansa Musa, ruler of the Mali Empire, makes the pilgrimage to Mecca with a vast caravan carrying large amounts of gold. In Cairo he spends and gives away so much gold that, according to Arab writers, its value there stays low for years. He returns with Muslim scholars and the poet and architect al-Sahili, who is traditionally credited with Timbuktu's Djinguereber Mosque.
significance: The journey made Mali famous in the Islamic world and in Europe, where a 1375 Catalan map shows Musa holding a gold nugget, and it helped Timbuktu grow into a center of Islamic learning.

title: Tenochtitlan founded
summary: According to Aztec tradition, the Mexica people end a long migration when they see an eagle perched on a cactus on an island in Lake Texcoco, the sign their god had promised, and found Tenochtitlan there. The traditional date may not be exact. They build the city on reclaimed marshland, with causeways to the shore and raised farm plots called chinampas.
significance: Tenochtitlan became the capital of the Aztec Empire and one of the largest cities in the world by 1500; Mexico City is built on its ruins, and the eagle and cactus appear on Mexico's flag.

title: Ashikaga (Muromachi) shogunate
summary: The Ashikaga established a military government based in Kyoto. Its authority weakened as regional lords gained power, and the regime ended when Oda Nobunaga expelled the last Ashikaga shogun.
significance: Its patronage shaped Japanese arts such as Noh theater, ink painting and the tea ceremony, while its weakness led to a century of civil war.

title: Vijayanagara Empire
summary: Founded in 1336, the Vijayanagara Empire united southern India under Hindu kings ruling from a vast capital on the Tungabhadra River. It grew rich on trade in spices, cotton and horses until its army was defeated by the Deccan sultanates at Talikota in 1565.
significance: For more than two centuries it was the great power of southern India and a patron of Hindu temple building and of literature in several languages.

title: Hundred Years' War
summary: English and French rulers fought intermittent wars over the French crown and territorial claims. The conflict strengthened royal authority in France, weakened English continental power, and transformed warfare.
significance: The war helped forge separate French and English national identities and ended the era in which English kings ruled large parts of France.

title: Black Death

location.name: Messina, Sicily (where it reached western Europe in 1347)

summary: Plague, caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis and spread by fleas and possibly from person to person, reaches Europe from the lands around the Black Sea, probably on Genoese trading ships, and arrives in Sicily in October 1347. Within four years it sweeps across Europe, the Middle East and North Africa, killing perhaps a third to a half of Europe's population, though the death toll is debated.
significance: The loss of so many people raised the value of labor, weakened serfdom in western Europe and shook faith in authority, and plague kept returning in waves for over three centuries.

title: Ming dynasty
summary: The Ming drove out the Mongols and restored Chinese rule. Its emperors built the Forbidden City, rebuilt the Great Wall in its present form and sent Zheng He's fleets across the Indian Ocean, while population, commerce and the porcelain and silk trades grew strongly.
significance: The Ming gave China nearly three centuries of stability and prosperity, and its goods were in demand across the world, drawing in much of the silver mined in the Americas.

title: Timur's conquests
summary: Timur (Tamerlane), a Turkic-Mongol chief, takes power in Transoxiana in 1370 and rules from Samarkand. Over three decades of campaigns he defeats the Golden Horde, sacks Delhi and Baghdad, defeats the Ottomans at Ankara in 1402, and dies in 1405 while marching on Ming China.
significance: His campaigns were extremely destructive and killed very large numbers of people, though estimates are uncertain, while the wealth and craftsmen he brought to Samarkand made it a showcase of Timurid art and architecture.

title: Timurid Empire
summary: Timur, known in Europe as Tamerlane, conquered an empire from Anatolia to India in campaigns of great destruction. His descendants ruled Central Asia and Iran from Samarkand and Herat and presided over a brilliant age of architecture, painting and astronomy.
significance: The Timurid courts set the standard for Persianate art and learning, and a Timurid prince, Babur, went on to found the Mughal Empire in India.

title: Jikji, oldest book printed with metal type
summary: At a temple in Cheongju, in the Korean kingdom of Goryeo, monks print a collection of Zen Buddhist teachings using movable type cast in metal. One volume survives, in the National Library of France.
significance: It is the oldest surviving book printed with movable metal type, made about 78 years before Gutenberg's Bible.

title: Kingdom of Kongo
summary: The Kingdom of Kongo lay south of the lower Congo River, in what is now Angola and the two Congos. After the Portuguese arrived in 1483 its kings adopted Christianity and exchanged ambassadors with Portugal and the pope, but the slave trade and civil wars weakened the kingdom.
significance: Kongo was one of the largest states of central Africa and among the first in Africa south of the Sahara to deal with Europeans as an equal.

title: Joseon Korea
summary: Founded by Yi Seong-gye, the Joseon dynasty ruled Korea for five centuries from Hanseong, modern Seoul, as a Confucian state run by scholar-officials. King Sejong introduced the Hangul alphabet in the 15th century, and the kingdom survived Japanese and Manchu invasions.
significance: Joseon shaped Korea's language, borders, social customs and Confucian values to this day.

title: Zheng He's treasure voyages
summary: On the orders of the Yongle Emperor, the admiral Zheng He, a Muslim court eunuch, leads seven great voyages with fleets of hundreds of ships, including dozens of large treasure ships, and tens of thousands of men. They sail through Southeast Asia to India, Arabia and the coast of East Africa, collecting tribute and displaying Ming power; the size of the largest treasure ships is debated.
significance: The voyages showed that China had the ships and skill for long ocean voyages decades before the Portuguese reached the Indian Ocean, but the Ming court ended them and China did not follow them with overseas expansion.

title: Forbidden City completed
summary: The Yongle Emperor of the Ming dynasty moves his capital from Nanjing to Beijing and has a walled palace city built there over fourteen years by hundreds of thousands of workers. It holds about 980 buildings ranged along a north-south axis, and ordinary people are forbidden to enter.
significance: It was the home of 24 emperors and the center of Chinese government until 1912, and it is the largest surviving palace complex in the world.

title: Aztec Empire
summary: The Aztec Empire was an alliance of three city-states led by the Mexica of Tenochtitlan, an island city of perhaps 200,000 people. It dominated central Mexico through tribute and war until Hernán Cortés and his Indigenous allies destroyed it in 1521.
significance: It was the dominant power of Mesoamerica when the Spanish arrived, and Mexico City stands on the ruins of its capital.

title: Inca Empire
summary: From Cusco the Inca built an empire stretching some 4,000 kilometers along the Andes, held together by roads, storehouses, labor service and records kept on knotted cords. Civil war and epidemic disease had weakened it when the Spanish under Pizarro arrived in 1532.
significance: It was the largest state in the Americas before European contact, governed without writing, wheels or money.

title: Pachacuti builds the Inca Empire
summary: After defending Cusco against an attack by the rival Chanka people, the Inca ruler Pachacuti, according to tradition, takes the throne and begins turning his small kingdom into an empire. He rebuilds Cusco and, with his son Topa Inca, conquers much of the Andes; the 1438 date comes from Spanish-era chronicles and is uncertain.
significance: The Inca Empire became the largest state in the Americas before Columbus, stretching some 4,000 km along the Andes, linked by a great road network and run with knotted cords called quipu for record-keeping instead of writing.

title: Gutenberg's printing press
summary: Johannes Gutenberg develops a printing press that combines movable metal type, oil-based ink and a screw press. His Bible, finished around 1455, is the first major book printed this way in Europe.
significance: Cheap printed books spread literacy and new ideas across Europe, helping drive the Reformation, the Scientific Revolution and the Enlightenment.

title: King Sejong creates Hangul
summary: King Sejong of Joseon devises an alphabet of 28 letters for writing Korean, so that ordinary people who cannot learn Chinese characters can read and write. The shapes of the consonants are based on the position of the mouth and tongue when making each sound. Scholars at court resist it, and it comes into general use only centuries later.
significance: Hangul is one of the few writing systems whose inventor and date are known, and it is praised by linguists for its design; it is the script of both Koreas today.

title: Fall of Constantinople
summary: After a siege of nearly two months, the 21-year-old Ottoman sultan Mehmed II captures Constantinople, using huge cannons to batter its ancient land walls. The last Byzantine emperor, Constantine XI, is believed to have died in the final assault.
significance: The fall ended the Byzantine Empire, the last remnant of the Roman Empire, and the city, later known as Istanbul, became the Ottoman capital; Greek scholars who fled west added to the Renaissance in Italy.

title: Songhai Empire
summary: Under Sonni Ali and Askia Muhammad, Songhai expanded from Gao on the Niger to rule most of the western Sahel, including Timbuktu and Djenne. A Moroccan army with firearms defeated it at Tondibi in 1591.
significance: It was the last and largest of the great West African trading empires, and under it Timbuktu was at its height as a center of Islamic scholarship.

title: Onin War
summary: A succession dispute and rival coalitions of Japanese lords devastated Kyoto. The conflict undermined central authority and is commonly used to mark the start of the Sengoku period.
significance: It destroyed the authority of the Ashikaga shoguns and opened more than a century of civil war in Japan.

title: Sengoku: Japan's Warring States
summary: Regional daimyo competed for power as shogunal authority fractured. Oda Nobunaga, Toyotomi Hideyoshi, and Tokugawa Ieyasu progressively reunified Japan. This band uses the Onin War through the Tokugawa shogunate; other definitions end in 1568, 1573, or 1615.
significance: The wars swept away the old order and ended with Japan reunified under a central government that kept the peace for 250 years.

title: Columbus reaches the Americas
summary: Christopher Columbus, a Genoese navigator sailing for the Spanish monarchs Ferdinand and Isabella, crosses the Atlantic with three ships, hoping to reach Asia by sailing west. He lands on an island in the Bahamas that its Taino inhabitants call Guanahani, then visits Cuba and Hispaniola, believing he has reached the Indies.
significance: His voyages began lasting contact between Europe and the Americas, leading to European conquest and colonization, catastrophic epidemics among Indigenous peoples, and the Columbian Exchange of crops, animals and diseases between the hemispheres.

title: Vasco da Gama reaches India
summary: The Portuguese navigator Vasco da Gama sails around the Cape of Good Hope and up the East African coast, then crosses the Indian Ocean with the help of a local pilot to reach Calicut, on India's Malabar Coast. His return to Lisbon with spices in 1499 shows that Europeans can reach Asia by sea.
significance: The route let Portugal, and later other European powers, trade directly with Asia by sea, bypassing Venetian and Middle Eastern middlemen, and began a European presence in the Indian Ocean that led to colonial empires.

title: High Renaissance in Italy
summary: Around 1500, the Renaissance revival of classical learning and art in Italy reaches its height, with Leonardo da Vinci, Michelangelo and Raphael all working in Florence and Rome. Within a few decades Leonardo paints the Mona Lisa, Michelangelo carves his David and paints the Sistine Chapel ceiling, and Raphael decorates the papal rooms in the Vatican.
significance: The High Renaissance set standards for painting, sculpture and architecture that artists across Europe imitated for generations, and its works remain among the most famous in the world.

title: Safavid Empire
summary: Shah Ismail I united Iran in 1501 and made Twelver Shia Islam its state religion. His successors fought the Ottomans and the Uzbeks, and under Shah Abbas I the capital Isfahan became one of the most beautiful cities in the world.
significance: The Safavids restored Iran as a single state within roughly its modern borders and made it the Shia country it remains.

title: Portuguese take Malacca
summary: A Portuguese fleet under Afonso de Albuquerque captures Malacca, a rich sultanate on the Malay Peninsula that controls the narrow strait between the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea. The Portuguese build a fortress there, and the sultan's family withdraws to found new states, including Johor.
significance: Malacca gave Portugal a base for the spice trade with the Moluccas and trade with China, and was one of the earliest European colonial footholds in Southeast Asia until the Dutch took it in 1641.

title: Luther's Ninety-five Theses
summary: Martin Luther, a monk and professor of theology, writes the Ninety-five Theses attacking the sale of indulgences, certificates that the Church said would reduce punishment for sins after death. He sends them to the Archbishop of Mainz, and according to a story first told after Luther's death he also nails them to the door of the Castle Church in Wittenberg. Printed copies spread across Germany within weeks.
significance: The protest grew into the Protestant Reformation, which split Western Christianity, led to more than a century of religious wars, and reshaped the politics and culture of Europe.

title: Protestant Reformation
summary: Reformers challenged Catholic authority and founded new Christian traditions, reshaping European politics, education, and worship. The band uses Luther's 1517 challenge through the Peace of Westphalia; historians use different endpoints.
significance: It ended the religious unity of Western Europe, led to more than a century of religious wars, and encouraged literacy and new ideas about individual conscience.

title: First circumnavigation of the globe

location.name: Seville (start and end of the voyage)

summary: Ferdinand Magellan, a Portuguese captain in Spanish service, leaves Seville with five ships and about 270 men to reach the Spice Islands by sailing west. He finds a strait around the tip of South America, crosses the Pacific and is killed in the Philippines in 1521. Juan Sebastián Elcano brings one ship, the Victoria, back to Spain in 1522 with 18 of the original crew.
significance: The voyage proved that a ship could sail around the world and showed Europeans the vast size of the Pacific and of the Earth.

title: Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire
summary: A small Spanish force led by Hernán Cortés, allied with tens of thousands of Indigenous warriors from Tlaxcala and other peoples who resent Aztec rule, captures Tenochtitlan after a long siege. A smallpox epidemic brought by the Europeans has already killed many of the city's people, including the emperor Cuitlahuac.
significance: The conquest destroyed the Aztec Empire and created New Spain, which became the center of Spanish rule in North America and brought Spanish language, Catholicism and silver mining to Mexico.

title: New Spain
summary: After the conquest of the Aztec Empire, Spain governed Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean, the Philippines and much of what is now the United States as the Viceroyalty of New Spain, ruled from Mexico City. Its silver mines supplied much of the world's coinage.
significance: Three centuries of Spanish rule gave the region its language, religion and institutions, and it ended with Mexican independence in 1821.

title: Transatlantic slave trade
summary: In the mid-1520s the first recorded slave voyages sail directly from Africa to the Americas, beginning a trade that grows to an enormous scale. Over more than three centuries, European and American traders, buying captives from African states and merchants, carry about 12.5 million Africans across the Atlantic, of whom around 10.7 million survive the voyage. Most are forced to work on plantations and in mines, above all in Brazil and the Caribbean.
significance: The trade devastated many African societies, built much of the wealth of the Atlantic economy, and created large African-descended populations across the Americas, along with lasting legacies of racism.

title: Mughal Empire
summary: Founded by Babur, the Mughal dynasty ruled most of the Indian subcontinent at its height under Akbar, Jahangir, Shah Jahan and Aurangzeb. It governed tens of millions of people through an efficient revenue system and built monuments such as the Taj Mahal and the Red Fort.
significance: The Mughal Empire was among the richest states in the world, and its blend of Persian and Indian culture shaped the art, cuisine and languages of South Asia.

title: Babur founds the Mughal Empire
summary: Babur, a Timurid prince from Central Asia who rules Kabul, invades northern India and defeats Ibrahim Lodi, the last Delhi sultan, at the First Battle of Panipat, using field guns and matchlock muskets against a much larger army with war elephants. He takes Delhi and Agra and founds the Mughal dynasty.
significance: The Mughal Empire went on to rule most of the Indian subcontinent, especially under Akbar and his successors, and its blend of Persian, Central Asian and Indian culture left monuments such as the Taj Mahal.

title: Spanish conquest of the Inca Empire
summary: Francisco Pizarro, with fewer than 200 Spanish soldiers, ambushes and captures the Inca emperor Atahualpa at Cajamarca, in the Andes of northern Peru. The empire is already weakened by civil war and by smallpox; Atahualpa pays a huge ransom in gold and silver but is executed in 1533, and the Spanish take Cusco the same year.
significance: Inca resistance continued until 1572, but the conquest brought the Andes under Spanish rule, and the silver of Peru and Bolivia soon flowed into the world economy.

title: Copernicus puts the Sun at the center
summary: Nicolaus Copernicus, a Polish astronomer and church canon, publishes On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres shortly before his death. It argues that the Earth and the other planets orbit the Sun, rather than everything circling a fixed Earth as most astronomers since Ptolemy had held.
significance: His Sun-centered model, later improved by Kepler and defended by Galileo, helped launch the Scientific Revolution and changed how people understood their place in the universe.

title: Manila galleon trade begins

location.name: Cebu (first Spanish base; Manila became the hub from 1571)

summary: Sailing from Cebu, the first Spanish base in the Philippines, the navigator Andrés de Urdaneta finds a return route east across the Pacific to Acapulco, opening regular trade between Asia and Spanish Mexico. After Miguel López de Legazpi makes Manila the capital of the Spanish Philippines in 1571, it becomes the hub of the trade, and galleons, usually one or two a year, carry American silver west and Chinese silk and porcelain east.
significance: Lasting until 1815, the route was one of the first regular trade links across the Pacific and, with Atlantic shipping, tied the Americas, Asia and Europe into a global trading network.

title: Azuchi-Momoyama period
summary: Nobunaga and Hideyoshi consolidated power during the final stages of Japanese reunification. This cultural and political period overlaps with Sengoku; its start is also often dated to 1573.
significance: In these decades Japan was reunified, its castles and castle towns were built, and the foundations of the Tokugawa order were laid.

title: Morocco defeats Songhai
summary: A Moroccan army of a few thousand men, many armed with muskets and led by Judar Pasha, crosses the Sahara and defeats the much larger army of the Songhai ruler Askia Ishaq II at Tondibi, near Gao. The Moroccans then occupy Gao, Timbuktu and Djenne.
significance: The defeat broke up the Songhai Empire, and the region split into smaller states while Timbuktu's trade and scholarship declined.

title: Japanese invasions of Korea (Imjin War)
summary: Toyotomi Hideyoshi, having reunified Japan, sends more than 150,000 soldiers to Korea as a first step toward conquering Ming China. They overrun most of the peninsula, but Admiral Yi Sun-sin's fleet cuts their supply lines, Korean irregulars harass them, and a Ming army comes to Korea's aid. The Japanese withdraw after Hideyoshi's death in 1598.
significance: The war devastated Korea, drained the Ming treasury on the eve of the Manchu rise, and left lasting bitterness between Korea and Japan.

title: Battle of Sekigahara
summary: Two years after Hideyoshi's death, the lords of Japan divide into two camps and meet in battle in a mountain valley. Tokugawa Ieyasu's eastern army defeats the western army of Ishida Mitsunari in a single day, helped by commanders who change sides during the fighting.
significance: The victory made Ieyasu master of Japan and led to the Tokugawa shogunate, which kept the country at peace for more than 250 years.

title: British Empire
summary: From trading companies and settlements founded in the 17th century, Britain built an empire that by 1920 covered about a quarter of the world's land and people, including India, much of Africa, Canada and Australia. Most of it became independent between 1947 and the 1960s.
significance: It was the largest empire in history and spread the English language, common law, parliamentary government and industrial capitalism, along with the lasting harms of conquest and colonial rule.

title: English East India Company founded
summary: Queen Elizabeth I grants a royal charter to a company of London merchants, giving it a monopoly on English trade east of the Cape of Good Hope. The company starts by trading in spices, then turns to cotton cloth, silk, indigo and later tea, building trading posts in India such as Surat, Madras, Bombay and Calcutta.
significance: From the 1750s the company used its own army to conquer much of India, which it governed until the British Crown took over in 1858.

title: Tokugawa (Edo) shogunate
summary: The Tokugawa military government ruled from Edo through a system of domains controlled by daimyo. It sustained a long period of internal peace, urban growth, and regulated foreign contact before the Meiji Restoration ended shogunal rule.
significance: It gave Japan more than 250 years of peace and a flourishing urban culture, and the society it shaped was the one that modernized so rapidly after 1868.

title: Thirty Years' War
summary: A revolt by Protestant nobles in Bohemia, begun when they throw two royal governors and their secretary out of a window in Prague, grows into a war involving most of the powers of Europe. Fought mainly in the German lands of the Holy Roman Empire, it mixes religious conflict between Catholics and Protestants with rivalry between the Habsburgs, France and Sweden.
significance: Estimates of the dead, mostly from disease and famine, range from about 4.5 to 8 million, and the Peace of Westphalia that ended the war in 1648 is often seen as shaping the modern idea of sovereign states.

title: Dutch found Batavia
summary: Jan Pieterszoon Coen of the Dutch East India Company (VOC) captures the port of Jayakarta on Java, destroys it, and builds a fortified town on its ruins named Batavia. It becomes the company's headquarters in Asia.
significance: Batavia was the center of Dutch trade and colonial rule in the region for over 300 years, and as Jakarta it became the capital of independent Indonesia.

title: Taj Mahal built
summary: The Mughal emperor Shah Jahan orders a white marble tomb at Agra for his favorite wife, Mumtaz Mahal, who died in childbirth in 1631. Thousands of craftsmen work on it for about two decades, with the main tomb finished around 1643 and the surrounding gardens and buildings around 1653.
significance: The Taj Mahal is often considered the finest example of Mughal architecture, which blends Persian, Indian and Islamic styles, and it is one of the most visited monuments in the world.

title: Sakoku: Japan closed to the West
summary: Fearing Christianity and foreign influence, the Tokugawa shoguns expelled the Portuguese, banned Japanese from travelling abroad and confined European trade to a small Dutch post on an island in Nagasaki harbor. Trade continued with China, Korea and the Ryukyu Islands under close control.
significance: Two centuries of managed isolation gave Japan internal peace and a distinctive culture, and ended only when American warships forced the country open.

title: Qing dynasty
summary: The Manchus, a people from the northeast, conquered China after 1644 and ruled it as the Qing dynasty. Under the Kangxi and Qianlong emperors the empire doubled in size, taking in Mongolia, Xinjiang, Tibet and Taiwan; in the 19th century rebellion and foreign pressure weakened it.
significance: It was China's last imperial dynasty, and the territory it ruled is largely that of China today.

title: High Qing era
summary: Under three long-reigning emperors, Kangxi, Yongzheng and Qianlong, the Qing dynasty was at its height. The empire doubled in territory, the population more than doubled to about 300 million, and Chinese silk, tea and porcelain were in demand around the world.
significance: It was the last great age of imperial China; by its end, population pressure and corruption were building toward the crises of the 19th century.

title: Siege of Vienna
summary: A large Ottoman army under the Grand Vizier Kara Mustafa Pasha besieges Vienna, the capital of the Habsburgs. On 12 September a relief army of imperial, German and Polish troops under the Polish king Jan III Sobieski attacks and routs the besiegers.
significance: The defeat began a long Ottoman retreat in central Europe, and by 1699 the Habsburgs had won most of Hungary from the Ottomans.

title: Enlightenment (approx.)
summary: Thinkers debated reason, scientific inquiry, liberty, and political authority. These ideas influenced reform and revolution across Europe and beyond. The dates are a broad editorial convention, not a single movement's formal beginning and end.
significance: Its ideas about rights, reason and government by consent inspired the American and French revolutions and remain the basis of modern liberal democracy.

title: Newton's Principia
summary: Isaac Newton, a professor at Cambridge, publishes the Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica (Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy). In it he sets out three laws of motion and the law of universal gravitation, showing that the same force that makes objects fall to the ground keeps the Moon and planets in their orbits.
significance: The Principia became the foundation of classical physics and a model for explaining nature through mathematical laws, central to the Scientific Revolution and the Enlightenment.

title: Battle of Plassey
summary: Robert Clive, commanding a small army of the British East India Company, defeats Siraj ud-Daulah, the Nawab of Bengal, near the village of Plassey. The result is largely settled before the fighting, as Clive has secretly won over the Nawab's commander Mir Jafar, whom he then installs as the new Nawab.
significance: The victory gave the company control over Bengal, one of India's richest provinces, and began the British conquest of India.

title: Industrial Revolution
summary: Beginning in Britain, new machines powered by water and then steam turn spinning and weaving into factory work, while coal mining and iron making grow sharply. Workers move from farms into fast-growing industrial towns such as Manchester. Historians debate the exact dates and how sudden the change was.
significance: Industrialization spread to continental Europe, North America and Japan in the 1800s and later to much of the world, bringing sustained economic growth along with urbanization, pollution and new social conflicts.

title: Watt's steam engine
summary: James Watt, an instrument maker in Glasgow, patents a separate condenser that makes the existing Newcomen steam engine far more efficient, because its main cylinder no longer has to be cooled at every stroke. In partnership with the Birmingham manufacturer Matthew Boulton, he later develops engines that can turn wheels and drive machinery.
significance: Watt's engines made steam power practical across many industries and became a driving force of the Industrial Revolution, and the unit of power, the watt, is named after him.

title: American Declaration of Independence
summary: During a war between Britain and thirteen of its American colonies, the Continental Congress in Philadelphia adopts the Declaration of Independence, drafted mainly by Thomas Jefferson. It declares that all men are created equal, with rights to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness, and that the colonies are now free and independent states.
significance: After the colonists won the war in 1783, the United States became a republic whose ideals of rights and self-government inspired revolutions elsewhere, though at first they did not extend to enslaved people, women or Native Americans.

title: United States
summary: Thirteen British colonies declared independence in 1776 and formed a federal republic under a written constitution. The country expanded across North America, fought a civil war over slavery, industrialized, and after 1945 was one of two superpowers and then the only one.
significance: Its constitution and ideals of rights and self-government influenced democracies around the world, and in the 20th century it became the world's leading economic and military power.

title: First Fleet arrives in Australia
summary: Eleven British ships carrying about 1,400 people, more than half of them convicts, arrive at Botany Bay and move on to Sydney Cove, where Captain Arthur Phillip founds a penal colony. The land is already home to Aboriginal peoples, including the Eora, whose ancestors have lived in Australia for at least 50,000 years.
significance: The colony began British settlement of Australia, which brought devastating losses of land and life to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples; 26 January is now Australia Day and, for many, also a day of mourning.

title: French Revolution
summary: With France bankrupt, King Louis XVI calls the Estates-General, and the deputies of the commoners declare themselves a National Assembly. Parisians storm the Bastille fortress on 14 July, and the Assembly abolishes feudal privileges and issues the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen.
significance: Over the next decade the revolution abolished the monarchy, executed the king, went through the Terror and spread through war, and its ideals of liberty, equality and national sovereignty reshaped politics around the world.

title: Dream of the Red Chamber published
summary: The novel by Cao Xueqin, who died in poverty in the 1760s leaving it unfinished, is printed for the first time in a 120-chapter version completed by other hands. It follows the decline of a great aristocratic family through the eyes of its young heir and the women around him.
significance: It is generally regarded as the greatest Chinese novel, with a whole field of scholarship devoted to it.

title: Haitian Revolution
summary: Enslaved Africans in the French colony of Saint-Domingue, the richest sugar colony in the Caribbean, rise in revolt. Under leaders such as Toussaint Louverture and Jean-Jacques Dessalines, they defeat French, Spanish and British forces, including an army sent by Napoleon, and declare the independent nation of Haiti on 1 January 1804.
significance: Haiti became the second independent country in the Americas, after the United States, and a state founded by formerly enslaved people, which inspired the enslaved and alarmed slaveholders across the Atlantic world.

title: Macartney Embassy to China
summary: Lord Macartney, sent by Britain to ask for wider trade and a permanent ambassador in Beijing, is received by the Qianlong Emperor at his summer residence. The emperor refuses every request, writing to King George III that China has no need of Britain's manufactures.
significance: The failure showed how differently the two empires saw the world, and Britain's wish to open China's trade led within fifty years to the Opium War.

title: Dutch East Indies
summary: When the Dutch East India Company went bankrupt, the Dutch state took over its possessions in the Indonesian archipelago and extended its rule over the islands during the 19th century. The colony exported coffee, sugar, rubber and oil until Japan occupied it in 1942.
significance: Dutch rule drew together the many islands and peoples that became Indonesia, which won its independence in 1949.

title: Napoleonic Wars
summary: Napoleon's France fought shifting European coalitions in wars that redrew borders and mobilized large armies. His final defeat at Waterloo and the Congress of Vienna established a new European settlement.
significance: The wars spread the legal and administrative reforms of the French Revolution across Europe, stirred nationalism, and left Britain the leading world power for a century.

title: Latin American wars of independence
summary: With Spain occupied by Napoleon, local leaders across Spanish America set up their own governments from 1810, and long wars with Spanish forces follow. Led by figures such as Simón Bolívar in the north, José de San Martín in the south and, in Mexico, at first the priest Miguel Hidalgo, most of the mainland colonies win independence by 1826, while Brazil breaks away from Portugal in 1822.
significance: New countries including Mexico, Colombia, Venezuela, Peru, Chile and Argentina replaced three centuries of Spanish rule, though many inherited deep social inequalities and soon faced civil wars and military strongmen.

title: Waterloo and the Congress of Vienna
summary: Napoleon, back from exile, is finally defeated by British, Dutch, German and Prussian armies at Waterloo, in today's Belgium, in June 1815. At the Congress of Vienna, which finishes its work days before the battle, the victorious powers redraw the map of Europe, restoring old monarchies and seeking a balance of power.
significance: The settlement helped keep peace among Europe's great powers for decades, with no general European war until 1914, though it held back nationalist and liberal movements.

title: First Opium War
summary: When the Chinese official Lin Zexu destroys over a thousand tonnes of opium smuggled into Canton by British merchants, Britain sends warships. Its navy, including steam-powered gunboats, wins easily, and the Treaty of Nanjing forces China to pay compensation, open five ports to trade and give Hong Kong Island to Britain.
significance: It was the first of what Chinese call the 'unequal treaties' that opened China to Western powers on their terms, the start of what is often called China's 'century of humiliation'.

title: Treaty of Waitangi
summary: Representatives of the British Crown and over 40 Māori chiefs sign a treaty at Waitangi, in New Zealand's Bay of Islands, and copies are later signed by around 500 more chiefs. The English and Māori-language versions differ: in the English text the chiefs give up sovereignty, while the Māori text grants the British governance but guarantees the chiefs' full authority over their lands and treasures.
significance: The treaty is regarded as New Zealand's founding document, and disputes over its meaning and breaches, especially land seizures, remain central to the country's politics.

title: Revolutions of 1848 and the Communist Manifesto
summary: A wave of revolutions sweeps across Europe, starting in Sicily and Paris and spreading to the German states, the Austrian Empire and Italy, as liberals, nationalists and workers demand constitutions, national unity and reform. The same year Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels publish The Communist Manifesto in London, calling on the workers of the world to unite.
significance: Most of the revolutions were crushed within a year or two, but they ended the French monarchy and serfdom in the Austrian Empire, and the Manifesto became one of the most influential political texts of modern times.

title: Taiping Rebellion
summary: The Taiping movement challenged the Qing dynasty and established a rival state based in Nanjing. The resulting civil war devastated large parts of China and severely strained Qing rule.
significance: It was one of the deadliest wars in history, with perhaps 20 million or more dead, and it fatally weakened the Qing dynasty.

title: Perry's ships open Japan

location.name: Uraga, at the mouth of Edo Bay

summary: Commodore Matthew Perry of the United States Navy anchors four warships, two of them steamers, off Uraga and delivers a letter demanding that Japan open its ports. He returns the next year with a larger squadron, and the shogunate signs a treaty opening two ports to American ships.
significance: The treaties that followed ended Japan's seclusion and discredited the shogunate, leading to its overthrow in the Meiji Restoration fifteen years later.

title: Second Opium War
summary: Britain and France go to war with Qing China to force wider trade and diplomatic access. Their troops take Guangzhou and Tianjin, march on Beijing in 1860 and loot and burn the emperor's Old Summer Palace. China is made to legalize the opium trade, open more ports, admit foreign envoys to the capital and cede Kowloon to Britain.
significance: The defeat, while the Taiping Rebellion was still raging, exposed the weakness of the Qing and deepened foreign control over China's trade.

title: Indian Rebellion of 1857
summary: Indian soldiers (sepoys) of the East India Company's army mutiny at Meerut, angered partly by rumors that new rifle cartridges are greased with cow and pig fat, and march to Delhi, where they proclaim the aging Mughal emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar their leader. The revolt spreads across northern and central India before British forces suppress it in 1858, with great brutality on both sides.
significance: Britain ended the East India Company's rule and the Mughal dynasty and governed India directly as the British Raj; in India the rebellion is often remembered as a first war of independence.

title: British Raj
summary: After the rebellion of 1857 the British Crown took over the government of India from the East India Company. It ruled about two thirds of the subcontinent directly and the rest through princes, built railways and canals, and faced a growing nationalist movement.
significance: India was the centerpiece of the British Empire, and the end of the Raj in 1947 created India and Pakistan and began the wider end of European empires.

title: Darwin's On the Origin of Species
summary: Charles Darwin publishes On the Origin of Species, arguing that living things change over generations through natural selection, as individuals better suited to their environment survive and reproduce more. Drawing on his voyage on HMS Beagle and decades of research, he presents evidence that species descend from common ancestors. Alfred Russel Wallace had reached a similar idea independently, and their papers were presented together in 1858.
significance: Evolution by natural selection became the foundation of modern biology, and the book transformed debates about humanity's place in nature.

title: American Civil War
summary: After Abraham Lincoln is elected president, eleven Southern slave states secede from the United States and form the Confederacy, and war, fought mainly over slavery and its expansion, begins when Confederate forces fire on Fort Sumter in April 1861. After four years of fighting, including the Battle of Gettysburg in 1863, the Union defeats the Confederacy in 1865.
significance: The war preserved the Union and led to the end of slavery in the United States with the Thirteenth Amendment, at a cost of an estimated 620,000 to 750,000 soldiers' lives.

title: Empire of Japan
summary: After the Meiji Restoration, Japan was governed in the emperor's name under a constitution adopted in 1889. It industrialized rapidly, defeated China and Russia, and took Taiwan, Korea and Manchuria. In the 1930s the military took control and led the country into a war across Asia and the Pacific that ended in defeat in 1945.
significance: It was the first non-Western state to become a modern industrial and colonial power, and its expansion and defeat reshaped the whole of East Asia.

title: Meiji Japan
summary: The restoration of imperial government ended the Tokugawa regime and ushered in major administrative, military, educational, and industrial reforms. Japan developed into an imperial power during the Meiji emperor's reign.
significance: In a single generation Japan turned from a secluded feudal society into an industrial and military power, the first outside the West to do so.

title: Meiji Restoration
summary: Samurai from domains such as Satsuma and Chōshū overthrow the Tokugawa shogunate and restore power in the name of the young Emperor Meiji, who moves his court to Edo, renamed Tokyo. The new leaders abolish the feudal domains and the privileges of the samurai and rapidly adopt Western-style industry, schooling, an army and, in 1889, a constitution.
significance: Within decades Japan became an industrial and military power, defeating China in 1895 and Russia in 1905 and building an empire in Asia.

title: Suez Canal opens
summary: After ten years of construction by a French-led company under Ferdinand de Lesseps, the Suez Canal opens across the isthmus of Suez in Egypt, linking the Mediterranean and the Red Sea. It is built largely by Egyptian laborers, many of them conscripted, and has no locks.
significance: By letting ships sail between Europe and Asia without going around Africa, the canal cut thousands of kilometers from the voyage between Britain and India and became one of the world's most important trade routes.

title: Berlin Conference and the Scramble for Africa

location.name: Congo basin, near Kinshasa (representative; the conference met in Berlin)

summary: Representatives of fourteen states, mostly European, meet in Berlin at the invitation of the German chancellor Otto von Bismarck to agree rules for claiming African territory; no Africans are invited. Around the conference the powers recognize King Leopold II's personal claim to the Congo, and in the following decades European powers conquer and divide almost all of Africa, leaving only Ethiopia and Liberia independent by 1914.
significance: Colonial rule redrew Africa's map with borders that often ignored existing peoples and states, and most of those borders survive in today's African countries.

title: Indian independence movement
summary: Organized nationalist politics, mass protest, civil disobedience, and other forms of resistance challenged British rule. This band begins with the founding of the Indian National Congress and ends with independence and partition; earlier resistance preceded it.
significance: It ended British rule over a fifth of humanity, and its methods of mass non-violent protest inspired later movements for independence and civil rights.

title: First Sino-Japanese War
summary: Japan and Qing China go to war over control of Korea. Japan's modernized army and navy win every major battle, destroying the Chinese fleet at Weihaiwei. By the Treaty of Shimonoseki, China recognizes Korea's independence, pays a large indemnity and cedes Taiwan to Japan.
significance: The war showed that Japan had overtaken China as the leading power in East Asia and set off a scramble by foreign powers for concessions in China.

title: Boxer Rebellion
summary: A peasant movement in northern China, known to foreigners as the Boxers, attacks Chinese Christians and missionaries, and with the support of the Qing court besieges the foreign legations in Beijing for 55 days in 1900. An army of eight nations relieves the siege, loots the capital and imposes a huge indemnity.
significance: The humiliation destroyed what remained of the Qing dynasty's standing and pushed it into late reforms, a decade before it fell.

title: Wright brothers' first powered flight

location.name: Kill Devil Hills, near Kitty Hawk

summary: Orville and Wilbur Wright, bicycle makers from Ohio, make the first widely recognized controlled, sustained flights in a powered, heavier-than-air airplane at Kill Devil Hills, near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina. The first flight lasts 12 seconds and covers 37 meters, and the longest of the day's four flights about 59 seconds.
significance: Their way of controlling an aircraft in three dimensions laid the groundwork for modern aviation, which within decades transformed travel, trade and warfare.

title: Russo-Japanese War
summary: Japan and Russia fight over control of Manchuria and Korea. Japan opens with a surprise attack on the Russian fleet at Port Arthur, takes the fortress after a long siege, wins the land battle of Mukden and destroys a second Russian fleet in the Tsushima Strait in May 1905.
significance: It was the first victory of an Asian power over a European one in modern times; it gave Japan a free hand in Korea and shook the Russian monarchy.

title: Einstein's theory of relativity

location.name: Bern (where Einstein worked at the patent office)

summary: Albert Einstein, a 26-year-old clerk at the Swiss patent office in Bern, publishes four groundbreaking papers, including his special theory of relativity, which shows that measurements of time and space depend on the observer's motion, and the equation E = mc², linking mass and energy. In 1915 he extends it into the general theory of relativity, which explains gravity as the curving of space and time.
significance: Relativity overturned ideas about space and time that had stood since Newton, and it underlies modern physics and cosmology as well as technologies such as GPS.

title: Korea under Japanese rule
summary: Japan annexed Korea in 1910 and ruled it as a colony for 35 years. It built railways and industry to serve its own empire, suppressed the Korean independence movement and, in the 1930s and 1940s, tried to erase Korean identity while conscripting Koreans for labor and war.
significance: The colonial period left deep wounds that still trouble relations between Korea and Japan, and it ended with the peninsula divided.

title: Xinhai Revolution ends imperial China
summary: An army uprising in Wuchang, in central China, sparks revolts across the provinces against the Qing dynasty. Revolutionaries proclaim the Republic of China with Sun Yat-sen as provisional president, and in February 1912 the six-year-old emperor Puyi abdicates.
significance: The revolution ended more than 2,000 years of imperial rule in China, but the new republic soon broke apart under warlords, opening decades of conflict.

title: Republic of China
summary: The republic that replaced the Qing dynasty soon broke up among rival warlords. The Nationalist Party under Chiang Kai-shek reunified much of the country from Nanjing in 1928, then faced Japanese invasion and a civil war with the Communists, which it lost.
significance: It ended more than two thousand years of imperial rule in China; after 1949 its government continued on Taiwan.

title: World War I
summary: After a Bosnian Serb nationalist assassinates the Austrian Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo, alliances draw the great powers into war, with Germany, Austria-Hungary and the Ottoman Empire facing France, Russia, Britain and later Italy and the United States. Millions of soldiers die in the trench warfare of the Western Front and on other fronts, from machine guns, artillery and poison gas.
significance: Estimates of the dead, soldiers and civilians, range from about 15 to 22 million; the war destroyed the German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian and Ottoman empires, helped bring on the Russian Revolution and redrew the map of Europe and the Middle East.

title: Russian Revolution
summary: Strained by war, Russia erupts in revolution: in February (March in the Western calendar) strikes and mutinies in Petrograd force Tsar Nicholas II to abdicate, and a provisional government takes over. In October (November) the Bolsheviks under Vladimir Lenin seize power, and they win the civil war that follows by the early 1920s.
significance: The revolution created the first state ruled by a communist party, which became the Soviet Union, and its ideology and rivalry with the West shaped much of the 20th century.

title: March First Movement
summary: In Seoul, 33 religious and civic leaders sign a declaration of Korea's independence from Japan, and students read it aloud to a crowd. Peaceful demonstrations spread across the country and involve perhaps two million people before Japanese police and troops suppress them, killing thousands.
significance: The movement united Koreans behind independence and led to a provisional government in exile; South Korea marks 1 March as a national holiday.

title: May Fourth Movement
summary: Students in Beijing march to protest the decision of the Paris Peace Conference to hand Germany's rights in Shandong province to Japan rather than back to China. Strikes and boycotts spread to other cities, and the government refuses to sign the treaty.
significance: The protests gave their name to a wider movement that rejected Confucian tradition in favor of science, democracy and writing in everyday language, and out of which the Chinese Communist Party grew.

title: Chinese Communist Party founded
summary: Thirteen delegates, among them the young Mao Zedong, meet in secret in a house in Shanghai's French Concession, with two representatives of the Communist International, and found the Chinese Communist Party. They represent only about fifty members.
significance: Within three decades the party had won control of China, which it has governed ever since.

title: Soviet Union
summary: The Soviet Union was a federation of republics ruled by the Communist Party from Moscow, formed after the Russian Revolution and civil war. Under Stalin it industrialized by force at enormous human cost; it bore the main burden of defeating Nazi Germany and then competed with the United States in the Cold War.
significance: It was the first communist state and one of two superpowers, and its collapse in 1991 ended the Cold War.

title: Republic of Turkey founded
summary: After defeating Greek, Armenian, French and other forces in the Turkish War of Independence, the nationalist movement led by Mustafa Kemal abolishes the Ottoman sultanate and proclaims the Republic of Turkey, with Ankara as its capital. Kemal, later called Atatürk, becomes its first president.
significance: Atatürk's reforms, including the abolition of the caliphate in 1924, a secular legal system and a new Latin-based alphabet, remade Turkey as a secular nation-state.

title: Chinese Civil War
summary: Nationalist and Communist forces fought intermittently for control of China, with a major interruption during the war against Japan. Communist victory on the mainland led to the People's Republic of China, while the Nationalist government withdrew to Taiwan; later confrontations continued.
significance: The Communist victory created the People's Republic of China and left Taiwan under a separate government, a division that persists.

title: Discovery of penicillin
summary: At St Mary's Hospital in London, the Scottish bacteriologist Alexander Fleming notices that a mold, Penicillium, has killed the bacteria around it in a culture dish. He names the substance it produces penicillin, but only in the early 1940s do Howard Florey, Ernst Chain and their team at Oxford purify it and show that it can cure infections.
significance: Mass-produced from World War II onward, penicillin became one of the first widely used antibiotics, opening an era in which many once-deadly infections could be cured and saving many millions of lives.

title: Great Depression begins
summary: Share prices on the New York Stock Exchange crash, wiping out fortunes and shaking confidence. Bank failures, falling trade and collapsing prices follow, and by 1933 about a quarter of the US workforce is unemployed as the slump spreads around the world. Economists still debate how much the crash itself caused the depression that followed.
significance: The Depression lasted through much of the 1930s, led governments to take a larger role in managing economies, and fed the rise of extremist movements such as Nazism in Germany.

title: Mukden Incident
summary: Officers of the Japanese army stationed in Manchuria blow up a short stretch of a Japanese-owned railway near Mukden, blame Chinese troops, and use the incident as a pretext to occupy the whole of Manchuria. Tokyo's civilian government fails to rein them in.
significance: It began fourteen years of Japanese aggression in China, showed that the League of Nations could not stop a determined aggressor, and put the Japanese army beyond civilian control.

title: Manchukuo
summary: After seizing Manchuria, Japan set up a state there with Puyi, the last emperor of China, as its nominal ruler. Real power lay with the Japanese army, which developed the region's heavy industry for its own war effort. The state collapsed when the Soviet Union invaded in August 1945.
significance: Manchukuo was the model of a puppet state, recognized by few countries, and Japan's refusal to give it up led to its withdrawal from the League of Nations.

title: Long March

location.name: Zunyi (where Mao rose to leadership on the march)

summary: Surrounded by Nationalist armies in the southeast, the Chinese Communists break out and retreat for a year across some of the roughest country in China, covering thousands of kilometers before reaching Shaanxi in the northwest. Of about 86,000 who set out with the main force, fewer than one in ten arrive.
significance: The march saved the Communist movement from destruction, made Mao Zedong its leader, and became the founding legend of the People's Republic.

title: Nanjing Massacre
summary: After capturing Nanjing, then China's capital, Japanese troops spend about six weeks killing prisoners of war and civilians and raping women on a mass scale. Estimates of the dead range from tens of thousands to more than 300,000; a postwar tribunal put the number at over 200,000.
significance: It is the most notorious atrocity of the war in Asia, and disputes over how it is remembered still strain relations between China and Japan.

title: Second Sino-Japanese War

location.name: Marco Polo Bridge, near Beijing (where the war began)

summary: A clash between Chinese and Japanese troops near Beijing in July 1937 grows into a full invasion. Japan takes the coast, the great cities and the railways, but China's government retreats inland to Chongqing and fights on for eight years, tying down more than a million Japanese soldiers. From 1941 the war is part of World War II.
significance: It was the largest Asian war of the 20th century, with Chinese deaths estimated at 15 to 20 million; it left the Nationalist government exhausted and helped the Communists win the civil war.

title: World War II
summary: Germany under Adolf Hitler invades Poland on 1 September 1939, and Britain and France declare war; in Asia, Japan has been at war with China since 1937. The war spreads worldwide, with the Allies, led by Britain, the Soviet Union, the United States and China, fighting the Axis powers of Germany, Italy and Japan, until Germany surrenders in May 1945 and Japan in August.
significance: The deadliest conflict in history, it killed an estimated 70 to 85 million people, including about six million Jews murdered in the Holocaust, and left the United States and the Soviet Union as rival superpowers.

title: Korea divided at the 38th parallel
summary: As Japan surrenders, the United States proposes and the Soviet Union accepts a line along the 38th parallel to divide their zones of occupation in Korea. Meant to be temporary, the division hardens as the Cold War sets in, and in 1948 separate governments are proclaimed in Seoul and Pyongyang.
significance: The line became the border between two hostile states, led to the Korean War, and still divides the peninsula.

title: Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki
summary: The United States drops atomic bombs on the Japanese cities of Hiroshima on 6 August and Nagasaki on 9 August 1945, the only use of nuclear weapons in war to date. The bombs kill an estimated 150,000 to 246,000 people by the end of the year, most of them civilians, many from burns and radiation sickness.
significance: Japan announced its surrender days later, after the Soviet Union had also declared war on it, and the bombings opened the nuclear age; historians still debate whether they were necessary to end the war.

title: Indonesia declares independence
summary: Two days after Japan's surrender ends its wartime occupation of the Dutch East Indies, the nationalist leaders Sukarno and Mohammad Hatta proclaim Indonesia's independence in Jakarta. The Dutch try to restore colonial rule, and four years of war and negotiation follow until the Netherlands transfers sovereignty in December 1949.
significance: Indonesia, a nation of thousands of islands and hundreds of ethnic groups, became one of the world's most populous countries and the most populous Muslim-majority nation.

title: United Nations founded

location.name: San Francisco (where the UN Charter was signed)

summary: Delegates of 50 countries meeting in San Francisco sign the Charter of the United Nations in June 1945, and the organization formally comes into being on 24 October. It aims to prevent future wars, with a Security Council in which five major powers (the United States, the Soviet Union, Britain, France and China) hold permanent seats and a veto.
significance: With nearly every country now a member, the UN became the main forum for international diplomacy, peacekeeping and humanitarian work, though rivalry among the great powers often limits what it can do.

title: Cold War
summary: The United States, Soviet Union, and their allies competed through military alliances, nuclear deterrence, political confrontation, and proxy wars. Although placed in the Europe lane, the rivalry shaped events across the world.
significance: It divided the world into rival blocs for more than forty years, drove the nuclear arms race and the space race, and shaped the politics of nearly every country.

title: Independence and Partition of India
